newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa's NP opposition demands apology from Tutu.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa's NP opposition demands apology from Tutu.

text.p: South Africa's opposition National Party on Monday demanded an unconditional apology from Archbishop Desmond Tutu for having publicly criticised its testimony on apartheid to the Truth Commission he heads.
The party, which implemented apartheid in 1948 and began dismantling it four decades later, also gave an ultimatum for Tutu's deputy chairman on the commission, Alex Boraine, to quit.

The demands were contained in a letter to Tutu, in his capacity as chairman of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, from lawyers acting for the National Party which is led by apartheid reformer F.W. de Klerk.

The letter, accusing Tutu and Boraine of having violated legislation requiring commissioners to be impartial, referred to a news conference on May 15 during which they condemned de Klerk's testimony to the commission the previous day.

Tutu told the news conference among other things that he had nearly broken down in tears because de Klerk, under aggressive questioning from commission lawyer Glen Goosen, had not taken sufficient responsibility for apartheid-era abuses.

At the time the National Party said Tutu and Boraine had effectively found the party guilty of atrocities, and compared their tough treatment of de Klerk with the friendly handling of testimony from leaders of the African National Congress.
The commission was set up in 1995 to probe human rights abuses by all sides during the apartheid race war in the hope that revealing the truth would aid reconciliation.
But the National Party letter on Monday indicated that the bias allegations were overshadowing attempts at reconciliation.

"You are required to apologise unconditionally for your conduct at the press conference...and to undertake that in future you will comply with the provisions of the act which require you to be impartial," the letter told Tutu.

"Dr Boraine is required forthwith to resign...You are required to give the assurance that Goosen will in future not be involved in any of the commission's dealings with office-bearers of our client," the letter said.
The letter set a deadline of noon on Wednesday (June 4) for Tutu to respond, saying that if the demands were not met the National Party would take further legal action.
The party is already boycotting the commission because of its alleged bias.
De Klerk, speaking to a meeting of the Cape Town Press Club earlier on Monday, called the behaviour of Tutu and Boraine a very serious deviation which could not be rectified with "a few band-aids".

"A serious situation exists that...can only be rectified by cutting to the bone and by a totally new situation being created where trust can be restored in the process and activities of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission," he said.
A spokesman for Tutu said a meeting of the full commission would study the letter before any response was made.
Tutu, who was patron of an ANC-aligned group during the 1980s, has denied that he or his commission was anything but even-handed.

Some independent political analysts have described Tutu as clearly biased against the National Party. They said that while the party's history might justify his position, it meant the commission was unlikely to achieve genuine reconciliation.
The analysts said the commission had uncovered a great deal of apartheid dirty tricks but its major impact was likely to be as a propaganda victory for the ANC ahead of elections in 1999.
